newsitem.title: EGYPT: UBS sees fourth quarter U.S. growth round four pct.
newsitem.headline: UBS sees fourth quarter U.S. growth round four pct.

text.p: U.S. fourth quarter real GDP growth may be running at an annual rate of around four percent, driven by very high growth in disposable incomes and consumer spending, said Marc Hendriks, head of Swiss Bank Corp's economic research in London.

"The consensus view is around three percent. We anticipate it to move above four percent in coming months. That is a considerable break from the consensus view, which will have a market reaction," he told the annual congress of the InterArab Cambist Association.

When unemployment drops below six percent, inflationary wage pressures increase. This has been masked by retailers' reluctance to raise prices, with a resulting movement of resources from the corporate to the consumer sector. But companies may soon start to raise prices, he said.
"I think we are too complacent. Maybe the Federal Reserve has it right, but the risks they are taking seem to be increasing almost daily," he said.

"A modest tightening of 25 basis points (in interest rates) would not have brought the economy to its knees. We estimate 150 basis points is needed to bring the rate of growth below its (non-inflationary) potential and stave off inflationary risks."

Hendriks said he saw short-term dollar strength, but there were powerful downward threats in the longer term. "Beware of the dollar. Protect yourselves on the European crosses. Buy European volatility. If anything goes wrong volatility will explode."
The dollar is trading in increasingly and "almost unbelievably" narrow ranges against the mark and yen.

"Given the changes in the nature and structure of the foreign exchange market and the increasing access to information flows across the world, it is highly likely that volatilities in the foreign exchange market have been permanently reduced," he said.
"But don't expect them to stay at these (current) levels because lots of things are happening beneath the surface which could erupt and cause spikes in foreign exchange markets."
